Twice
TWYSE
adv.
From Middle English twies, from Anglo-Saxon twiges, the genitive of twa, two. Webster 1828: two times; once and again; doubly. Jude coins one of Scripture’s most alarming phrases with it, and Job uses it for the persistence of a God who speaks unheard.

Biblical Definition

Jude’s description of false teachers piles image on image and ends with a phrase that has no parallel: clouds they are without water, carried about of winds; trees whose fruit withereth, without fruit, twice dead, plucked up by the roots (Jude 1:12). Twice dead — dead in the trespasses and sins common to all men, and dead again in an apostasy that has abandoned the profession once made. The tree is not merely barren but uprooted. Job’s friend Elihu uses the word for divine persistence against human dullness: For God speaketh once, yea twice, yet man perceiveth it not (Job 33:14) — the failure is in the perceiving, not the speaking. The Pharisee in the parable offers his frequency as his credential: I fast twice in the week, I give tithes of all that I possess (Luke 18:12), and goes down to his house not justified. And Kings records a king repeatedly saved by a prophet’s warning: the king of Israel sent to the place which the man of God told him and warned him of, and saved himself there, not once nor twice (2 Kings 6:10).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines TWICE as two times; once and again; and also doubly, in twofold measure or degree.

expand to see more

TWICE, adv. — Two times.

Doubly; in twofold degree or quantity; as twice the amount.

Once and again; repeatedly.

TWICE-TOLD, a. — Related a second time; hence, stale or wearisome.

Anglo-Saxon twiges, from twa, two — the adverbial genitive, as in once and thrice.

Key Scripture

Jude 1:12 — "These are spots in your feasts of charity, when they feast with you, feeding themselves without fear: clouds they are without water, carried about of winds; trees whose fruit withereth, without fruit, twice dead, plucked up by the roots;"

Job 33:14 — "For God speaketh once, yea twice, yet man perceiveth it not."

Luke 18:12 — "I fast twice in the week, I give tithes of all that I possess."

2 Kings 6:10 — "And the king of Israel sent to the place which the man of God told him and warned him of, and saved himself there, not once nor twice."

Modern Corruption

The Pharisee’s I fast twice in the week is a true statement of genuine discipline offered as a ground of acceptance, which is why the parable ends with him unjustified.

expand to see more

Nothing the Pharisee says in Luke 18 is false. He did fast twice a week, beyond what the law required; he did tithe all his possessions; he was not an extortioner or an adulterer. The parable does not expose him as a hypocrite in the sense of a liar — it exposes the ground he stood on. He prayed with himself, thanked God that he was not as other men, and made his record the basis of his standing. The publican, who had no record to offer, smote his breast and asked God to be merciful to him a sinner, and went down to his house justified rather than the other. This is the doctrine of justification in a parable: the ground of acceptance is God’s mercy received by faith, never the believer’s attainment, however real that attainment may be. Real disciplines become deadly the moment they are offered as a claim.

Jude’s twice dead, plucked up by the roots is the sharpest description of apostasy in the New Testament, and it must be read alongside the Reformed doctrine of perseverance rather than against it. Jude is not describing believers who lost salvation; the whole letter distinguishes these men from the beloved who are preserved in Jesus Christ (Jude 1:1) and closes with the doxology to Him who is able to keep us from falling. They are men who crept in unawares, who feasted with the church without fear, and whose fruitlessness was finally exposed. 1 John 2:19 states the principle plainly: they went out from us, but they were not of us. The tree that is plucked up by the roots is shown never to have been rooted.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek dis (G1364), twice; apothnesko (G599), to die; ekrizoo (G1610), to root out; Hebrew paamayim, two times.

expand to see more

Greek dis (G1364) — twice; twice dead (Jude 1:12) and the Pharisee’s twice in the week (Luke 18:12).

Greek ekrizoo (G1610) — to uproot, to pluck up by the roots; the second half of Jude’s image.

Greek phthinoporinos (G5352) — of late autumn, when fruit should be present and is not; trees whose fruit withereth.

Hebrew paamayim — two times, twice; God speaketh once, yea twice (Job 33:14).

Hebrew shub (H7725) — to turn or return; the repeated warnings of 2 Kings 6:10.

Usage

"Twice dead, plucked up by the roots (Jude 1:12) — dead in sin, and dead again in abandoned profession."

"God speaketh once, yea twice, yet man perceiveth it not (Job 33:14) — the failure is in the perceiving."

"I fast twice in the week (Luke 18:12) — a true record offered as a ground, and he went down unjustified."
